det giver ikke mening.explanation: "Det giver ikke mening" means "that doesn't make sense". Word for word, it means "that gives no meaning". To say it makes no sense at all, add "slet" (at all): "Det giver slet ikke mening" (That makes no sense at all).

det går fint.explanation: "Det går fint" means "it's going fine". When someone asks how you are, you can answer: "Hvordan går det?" "Det går fint." (How is it going? It's going fine.) To say things are going badly, swap "fint" (fine) for "dårligt" (badly): "Det går dårligt" (It's going badly).

det går godt.explanation: "Det går godt" means "it's going well". When someone asks "Hvordan går det?" (How is it going?), you can answer "Det går godt." To ask the same question back, add "og dig?" (and you?): "Det går godt, og dig?" (I'm doing well, and you?)

det gør ikke noget.explanation: "Det gør ikke noget" means "it's okay". You say it when someone says "Undskyld" (Sorry): "Undskyld, jeg kom for sent." "Det gør ikke noget." (Sorry, I was late. It's okay.) Word for word, it means "it does not do anything". Do not mix it up with "det er lige meget" (it does not matter). You say that one when two options are equally fine to you: "Te eller kaffe?" "Det er lige meget." (Tea or coffee? It does not matter.)

det håber jeg.explanation: "Det håber jeg" means "I hope so". To answer a question about something that may happen, say: "Kommer Anna i morgen?" "Det håber jeg." (Is Anna coming tomorrow? I hope so.) Word for word, it means "that hope I".

det kan godt være.explanation: "Det kan godt være" means "that may be". To agree that the other person could be right and then give your own view, add "men" (but): "Det er for dyrt." "Det kan godt være, men jeg vil have den." (It is too expensive. That may be, but I want it.)

det kan man ikke vide.explanation: "Det kan man ikke vide" means "you never know". To answer a question about the future, say: "Bliver det sol i morgen?" "Det kan man ikke vide." (Will it be sunny tomorrow? You never know.) Word for word, it means "that can one not know".

det var dog utroligt.explanation: "Det var dog utroligt" means "that's incredible". When someone tells you surprising news, you can react: "Jeg vandt i lotto!" "Det var dog utroligt!" (I won the lottery! That's incredible!) The word "utroligt" is built from "u-" (un-) and "trolig" (likely).

det var på høje tid.explanation: "Det var på høje tid" means "it was high time". To tell someone they came late, say: "Det var på høje tid, at du kom!" (It was high time you showed up!) Word for word, it means "it was on high time".

det var så lidt.explanation: "Det var så lidt" means "you're welcome". When someone thanks you, you can answer: "Tak, fordi du hjalp mig!" "Det var så lidt." (Thank you for helping me! You're welcome.) Word for word, it means "it was so little".

det ved jeg ikke.explanation: "Det ved jeg ikke" means "I don't know". Word for word, it means "that know I not". "At vide" (to know) is for facts. To say you know a person or place, use "at kende" (to be familiar with) instead: "Jeg kender Peter" (I know Peter).

det vil sige.explanation: "Det vil sige" means "that is to say". To explain or sum up what you just said, put it before the explanation: "Jeg bor i Jylland, det vil sige i Aarhus" (I live in Jutland, that is to say in Aarhus). Word for word, it means "that will say". The short form in writing is "dvs." (i.e.).

detaljeret.explanation: "Detaljeret" means "detailed". It comes from the noun "en detalje" (a detail). To describe an explanation that gives every detail, say: "en detaljeret beskrivelse" (a detailed description).

dets.explanation: "Dets" means "its". When the thing belongs to a word that takes "et", such as "et værelse" (a room), say: "dets vindue" (its window). When the thing belongs to a word that takes "en", such as "en bil" (a car), use "dens" (its) instead: "dens motor" (its engine).

diabetes.explanation: "Diabetes" means "diabetes". It also appears in "svangerskabsdiabetes" (gestational diabetes), where "svangerskab" means "pregnancy".

diarré.explanation: "Diarré" means "diarrhea". To spell it in Danish, end it with "é" with an accent, not with "a" as in English.

diesel.explanation: "Diesel" means "diesel". To say you are filling the car with fuel, use "at tanke" (to fill up with fuel): "Jeg skal tanke diesel" (I need to fill up with diesel).

det tror jeg.explanation: "Det tror jeg" means "I think so". To answer a question when you believe the answer is yes, say: "Kommer Anna i dag?" "Det tror jeg." (Is Anna coming today? I think so.) Word for word, it means "that believe I".

det tror jeg ikke.explanation: "Det tror jeg ikke" means "I don't think so". To answer a question when you believe the answer is no, say: "Kommer Anna i dag?" "Det tror jeg ikke." (Is Anna coming today? I don't think so.) Word for word, it means "that believe I not".

det passer ikke.explanation: "Det passer ikke" means "that's not true". To correct a claim, say: "Du var der i går." "Det passer ikke." (You were there yesterday. That's not true.) To say a claim is true, leave out "ikke" (not): "Det passer" (That's true).

dig.explanation: "Dig" means "you". When you talk to one person who receives the action, use "dig": "Jeg ringer til dig" (I am calling you). When that person does the action, use "du" (you) instead: "Du ringer til mig" (You are calling me). To talk to several people, use "jer" (you, many): "Jeg ringer til jer" (I am calling you all).

digital.explanation: "Digital" means "digital". To describe a word that takes "et", add "t": "et digitalt ur" (a digital watch). Before a plural word, add "e": "digitale ure" (digital watches).

dild.explanation: "Dild" means "dill". To tell someone to chop the herb, say: "Hak dilden fint" (Chop the dill finely).

din.explanation: "Din" means "your". It goes with a word that takes "en", such as "en hat" (a hat): "din hat" (your hat). With a word that takes "et", say "dit": "dit værelse" (your room). Before more than one thing, say "dine": "dine nøgler" (your keys).

dine.explanation: "Dine" means "your". Use it before more than one thing: "dine nøgler" (your keys). For one thing that takes "en", say "din": "din nøgle" (your key). For one thing that takes "et", say "dit": "dit hus" (your house).

diplomatisk.explanation: "Diplomatisk" means "diplomatic". When you talk about how countries deal with each other, use it: "en diplomatisk krise" (a diplomatic crisis). When you want someone to handle a delicate situation with care, say: "Vær diplomatisk" (Be diplomatic).

direkte.explanation: "Direkte" means "straight". When you talk about a flight with no stop on the way, it means "direct": "et direkte fly" (a direct flight).

disciplin.explanation: "En disciplin" means "a discipline". When you talk about self-control, say: "Hun har stor disciplin" (She has great discipline). When you talk about one event in a sport, say: "Længdespring er en disciplin" (The long jump is an event).

diset.explanation: "Diset" means "hazy". It comes from the noun "en dis" (a haze). To say the weather is hazy, say: "Det er diset i dag" (It is hazy today).

diskret.explanation: "Diskret" means "discreet". To ask someone to keep something private, say: "Vær diskret" (Be discreet). When you describe a quiet style that does not stand out, it means "subtle": "en diskret farve" (a subtle color).

diskrimination.explanation: "Diskrimination" means "discrimination". To say the reason, use "på grund af" (because of): "diskrimination på grund af alder" (discrimination because of age).

disse.explanation: "Disse" means "these". When you point to one thing instead of several, use "denne" (this) for a word that takes "en": "denne sko" (this shoe). For a word that takes "et", use "dette" (this): "dette hus" (this house). "Disse" is formal. In everyday speech, "de her" (these) is the plain way to say it: "de her sko" (these shoes).

distraheret.explanation: "Distraheret" means "distracted". To name what distracts you, add "af" (by): "Jeg var distraheret af min telefon" (I was distracted by my phone).

dit.explanation: "Dit" means "your". It goes with a word that takes "et", such as "et værelse" (a room): "dit værelse" (your room). With a word that takes "en", say "din": "din bil" (your car). Before more than one thing, say "dine": "dine sko" (your shoes).

dna.explanation: "DNA" means "DNA". It takes "et", as the form "DNA'et" (the DNA) shows. To say the police found it somewhere, say: "Politiet fandt DNA på stedet" (The police found DNA at the scene).

dobbelt.explanation: "Dobbelt" means "double". To compare two ages, say: "Han er dobbelt så gammel som mig" (He is twice as old as me). It is also the first part of other words, such as "dobbeltværelse" (double room).

dog.explanation: "Dog" means "though". When you want to say "all the same", use it: "Det er dyrt, men jeg køber det dog" (It is expensive, but I am buying it anyway). When you want to make an invitation or request friendlier, use it: "Sæt dig dog" (Do sit down).

dokumentation.explanation: "Dokumentation" means "documentation". To say what the documentation belongs to, add "til" (for): "dokumentationen til programmet" (the documentation for the program).

dommedag.explanation: "Dommedag" means "doomsday". It is built from "en dom" (a verdict) and "en dag" (a day). To say that something is not a disaster, say: "Det er ikke dommedag" (It is not the end of the world).

doven.explanation: "Doven" means "lazy". To say how you feel today, say: "Jeg er doven i dag" (I am lazy today). The opposite is "flittig" (diligent): "Hun er flittig" (She is diligent).

dramatisk.explanation: "Dramatisk" means "dramatic". When you say that a person makes too much of things, say: "Du er så dramatisk!" (You are so dramatic!)

dressing.explanation: "En dressing" means "a dressing". To say what is in it, add "med" (with): "en dressing med hvidløg" (a dressing with garlic).

drikkepenge.explanation: "Drikkepenge" means "tip". Literally, it means "drink money", from "at drikke" (to drink) and "penge" (money). The word is used without an article. To tell a waiter to keep the change, say: "Tak, behold resten som drikkepenge" (Thanks, keep the change as a tip).

drikkevarer.explanation: "Drikkevarer" means "drinks". It is built from "at drikke" (to drink) and "varer" (goods). To talk about one single drink, say "en drik" (a drink): "en kold drik" (a cold drink).

dristig.explanation: "Dristig" means "bold". When you describe clothes that dare to be different, it means "daring": "en dristig kjole" (a daring dress).

du.explanation: "Du" means "you". When you talk to one person, say: "Er du træt?" (Are you tired?) Danes use "du" with older people and with a boss too. When that person receives the action, use "dig" (you): "Jeg ser dig" (I see you). To talk to several people, say "I" (you, many): "I er søde" (You are all sweet).

dug.explanation: "En dug" means "dew". When you talk about a cloth on a table, "en dug" is a different word: "en hvid dug" (a white tablecloth).

dum.explanation: "Dum" means "stupid". When you say it about a person, it sounds rude: "Du er dum" (You are stupid). To say a thing was stupid, add "t": "Det var dumt" (That was stupid).

dyb.explanation: "Dyb" means "deep". When you talk about sleep, use it: "en dyb søvn" (a deep sleep). When you talk about a voice, use it too: "en dyb stemme" (a deep voice).

dybtgående.explanation: "Dybtgående" means "thorough". It is built from "dybt" (deeply) and "gående" (going). When you talk about changes that go far, it means "profound": "dybtgående reformer" (profound reforms).

dygtig.explanation: "Dygtig" means "skilled". To name the skill, add "til" (at): "dygtig til sprog" (good at languages). To praise someone, say "Dygtig!" (Well done!)

dynamisk.explanation: "Dynamisk" means "dynamic". It comes from the noun "en dynamik" (dynamics). To describe a city that keeps changing, say: "en dynamisk by" (a dynamic city).

dyrebar.explanation: "Dyrebar" means "precious". It comes from the word "dyr" (expensive). To say that time is precious, say: "Tid er dyrebar" (Time is precious).

dyrevelfærd.explanation: "Dyrevelfærd" means "animal welfare". It is built from "et dyr" (an animal) and "velfærd" (welfare). To talk about farms, say: "dyrevelfærd i landbruget" (animal welfare in farming).

dårlig.explanation: "Dårlig" means "bad". To say how you feel, use "dårligt" with "have det" (to feel): "Jeg har det dårligt" (I feel bad). "Dårlig" has its own words for "worse" and "worst": "værre" (worse) and "værst" (worst).

dårlig til.explanation: "Dårlig til" means "bad at". It is built from "dårlig" (bad) and "til" (at). To ask someone what they are bad at, say: "Hvad er du dårlig til?" (What are you bad at?)

død.explanation: "Død" means "dead". When you talk about a device that has stopped working, use it too: "Min telefon er død" (My phone is dead).

dødbringende.explanation: "Dødbringende" means "deadly". It is built from "død" (death) and "bringende" (bringing). To talk about a danger, say: "et dødbringende virus" (a deadly virus). To say that people can die, use "dødelig" (mortal) instead: "Vi er alle dødelige" (We are all mortal).

dødelig.explanation: "Dødelig" means "deadly". When you talk about something that can kill, use it: "Svampen er dødelig" (The mushroom is deadly). When you talk about people who can die, it means "mortal": "Vi er alle dødelige" (We are all mortal).

dødkedelig.explanation: "Dødkedelig" means "deadly boring". It is built from "død" (dead) and "kedelig" (boring). The same "død-" in front of another word makes it extreme, as in "dødtræt" (dead tired).

dødsstraf.explanation: "En dødsstraf" means "a death penalty". It is built from "en død" (a death) and "en straf" (a punishment). To say a court gives it, use "at idømme" (to impose): "Retten idømte ham dødsstraf" (The court imposed the death penalty on him).

dømmekraft.explanation: "En dømmekraft" means "a judgment", as in good sense and not a court decision. It is built from "at dømme" (to judge) and "kraft" (power). To say a task needs good sense, say: "Det kræver dømmekraft" (It takes judgment).

døv.explanation: "Døv" means "deaf". To say someone hears a little, use "hørehæmmet" (hard of hearing) instead: "Min far er hørehæmmet" (My father is hard of hearing).

en dag.explanation: "En dag" means "a day". To say every day, use "hver dag" (every day). To greet someone, say "god dag" (hello). The names of the days of the week end in "-dag", such as "mandag" (Monday) and "tirsdag" (Tuesday).

en dagbog.explanation: "En dagbog" means "a diary". It is built from "dag" (day) and "bog" (book). To say you write a diary, use "at føre dagbog" (to keep a diary).

en daglig leder.explanation: "En daglig leder" means "a general manager". Literally, it means "a daily leader". To ask who runs the place, say: "Hvem er den daglige leder?" (Who is the general manager?)

en dagligvare.explanation: "En dagligvare" means "a grocery item". It is built from "daglig" (daily) and "en vare" (a product). To talk about groceries in general, use the plural: "Jeg køber dagligvarer" (I buy groceries).

en dagplejer.explanation: "En dagplejer" means "a home daycare provider". In Denmark, parents can choose one for the youngest children instead of "en vuggestue" (a daycare center for toddlers): "Vores datter går i vuggestue" (Our daughter goes to a daycare center).

en dagsorden.explanation: "En dagsorden" means "an agenda". It is built from "dag" (day) and "en orden" (an order). When you talk about topics that society is discussing, say: "noget er på dagsordenen" (something is on the agenda).

en dagsrejse.explanation: "En dagsrejse" means "a day trip". It is built from "dag" (day) and "rejse" (journey). To say where the trip goes, add "til" (to): "en dagsrejse til Skagen" (a day trip to Skagen).

en dal.explanation: "En dal" means "a valley". To say where a valley lies, say: "en dal mellem bjergene" (a valley between the mountains).

en dam.explanation: "En dam" means "a pond". To talk about a larger body of water, use "en sø" (a lake): "Vi svømmer i søen" (We swim in the lake).

en dame.explanation: "En dame" means "a lady". To mark the women's restroom, a door says "Damer" (ladies). To greet an audience, say: "Mine damer og herrer" (Ladies and gentlemen).

en dannelse.explanation: "En dannelse" means "an education", as in good manners and wide knowledge. To talk about school or job training, use "en uddannelse" (a training program) instead: "Jeg tager en uddannelse som elektriker" (I am training as an electrician). When you talk about how something comes into being, "dannelse" means "formation": "dannelsen af skyer" (the formation of clouds).

en dans.explanation: "En dans" means "a dance". It comes from the verb "at danse" (to dance). To ask someone to dance, say: "Må jeg få denne dans?" (May I have this dance?)

en danser.explanation: "En danser" means "a dancer". To say what someone does for a living, leave out "en": "Hun er danser" (She is a dancer).

en dansker.explanation: "En dansker" means "a Dane". To ask about someone's nationality, leave out "en": "Er du dansker?" (Are you a Dane?) For the language, use "dansk" (Danish): "Jeg taler dansk" (I speak Danish).

en dataanalytiker.explanation: "En dataanalytiker" means "a data analyst". To say what your job is, leave out "en": "Jeg er dataanalytiker" (I am a data analyst).

en database.explanation: "En database" means "a database". To say you look something up in it, say: "Jeg søger i databasen" (I am searching the database).

en date.explanation: "En date" means "a date", as in a romantic meeting. The word is borrowed from English. For a date on the calendar, use "en dato" (a calendar date): "Hvilken dato er det?" (What date is it?)

en dato.explanation: "En dato" means "a date (calendar)", such as 5 March. Do not mix it up with "en date" (a romantic meeting), which is borrowed from English: "Hun har en date i aften" (She has a date tonight).

en datter.explanation: "En datter" means "a daughter". To say "my daughter", use "min": "Min datter er syv år" (My daughter is seven years old).

en deadline.explanation: "En deadline" means "a deadline". The word is borrowed from English. A Danish word for the same thing is "en frist" (a time limit): "Fristen er fredag" (The deadline is Friday).

en debat.explanation: "En debat" means "a debate". To say you take part in one, use "at deltage i" (to take part in): "Hun deltager i debatten" (She takes part in the debate).

en debattør.explanation: "En debattør" means "a debater". It is built from "en debat" (a debate). To say what someone is, leave out "en": "Hun er debattør" (She is a debater).

en debut.explanation: "En debut" means "a debut". The matching verb is "at debutere" (to make your debut): "Hun debuterede som forfatter i 2010" (She made her debut as a writer in 2010).

en deciliter.explanation: "En deciliter" means "a deciliter". In writing, it is shortened to "dl": "2 dl mel" (2 deciliters of flour).

en definition.explanation: "En definition" means "a definition". After "definition", use "på" (of) and then the word being defined: "Hvad er definitionen på frihed?" (What is the definition of freedom?)

en dej.explanation: "En dej" means "a dough". For pancake batter, the Danish word is also "dej": "pandekagedej" (pancake batter).

en dekoration.explanation: "En dekoration" means "a decoration". The matching verb is "at dekorere" (to decorate): "Vi dekorerer stuen" (We are decorating the living room).

en del.explanation: "En del" means "a part". When you talk about how many people or things there are, it means "quite a lot": "Der er en del mennesker her" (There are quite a few people here).

en delfin.explanation: "En delfin" means "a dolphin". It is spelled with "e" and "f", not with "o" and "ph" as in English.

en delmængde.explanation: "En delmængde" means "a subset". It is built from "del" (part) and "en mængde" (a set).
